# Part 1: Motivation {background-color="#004D1E"}

## Ecosystem Services Under Pressure

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.82em; align-items: flex-start;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Context
- Ecosystem services — pollination, water regulation, coastal protection — are declining globally
- Land cover change, climate change, and habitat degradation are the primary drivers
- Billions of people depend on ecosystem services for food security, water supply, and climate regulation
- Losses are **geographically uneven**: some regions and populations bear a disproportionate burden

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Gaps in global change assessment
- *Where* is ES change most severe?
- *Who* bears the greatest burden of that change?
- *What* is driving it?
- Temporally explicit, spatially comparable, multi-service assessments remain scarce

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- The left column is the situation: we have global evidence that ES are declining and that billions depend on them. This is well-established.
- The right column is the gap that motivates this work: we lack the spatial granularity to answer where, who, and what at global scale simultaneously.
- Chaplin-Kramer et al. (2019 Science) quantified global NCP change for the first time. Our work extends it: 1992–2020 trend, hotspot detection, socioeconomic profiling, and attribution.
- ~2 min
:::

---

## Our Framework: Four Questions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}

### WHAT?
How has the provision of ecosystem services changed — in direction, magnitude across regions?

:::

::: {.column width="25%"}

### WHERE?
The geography of change — where is decline most intense?

:::

::: {.column width="25%"}

### WHO?
Which populations are most exposed to ES provision loss, and at what scale?

:::

::: {.column width="25%"}

### WHY?
Is monitoring land cover change alone enough to track where ES provision is declining most?

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- This four-pillar structure runs through the entire book and paper.
- WHAT: Path A, pixel-level global summaries.
- WHERE: Path B, 10km hotspot grid.
- WHO: KS socioeconomic profiling + serviceshed multiplier.
- WHY: Does land cover change alone capture where ES provision is declining most? Spatial co-occurrence of ES hotspots and LC conversion hotspots — the "monitoring gap" is the core finding.
:::

# Part 2: Methods {background-color="#004D1E"}

## Data Inputs: 1992 & 2020 Global Layers

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
::: {.column width="34%"}

### Ecosystem Services
**InVEST models, 300m**

- Nitrogen Export & Retention
- Sediment Export & Retention
- Pollination
- Coastal Risk & Protection
- Nature Access

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

### Land Cover
**ESA CCI + C3S, 300m**

- 1992 & 2020 endpoints
- Reclassified to 9 functional classes
- Source of both InVEST inputs and attribution analysis

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

### Socioeconomic
**Gridded, 2020**

- Population (GHS-POP)
- GDP
- Human Development Index
- Gini coefficient

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Time period: 1992–2020 (28 years). Land cover at endpoints only — no annual transitions.
- ESA CCI has a minor processing-chain discontinuity at the 2015/2016 version boundary — acknowledged as a limitation.
- Land cover serves a dual role: primary InVEST input AND baseline for the spatial attribution analysis.
:::

---

## Five Ecosystem Services Define the Hotspots

[Five hotspot-defining services across three thematic areas — all globally modelable with InVEST at consistent resolution.]{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

| Theme | Service | What it measures |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Habitat & Access** | Nature Access | Proximity to intact natural habitat — recreational, cultural, wellbeing value |
| | Pollination | Wild pollinator habitat support — food security for pollination-dependent crops |
| **Coastal Risk** | Coastal Risk | Wave energy reaching shore, net of habitat attenuation (mangroves, reefs, wetlands) |
| **Hydrological Regulation** | Nitrogen Export | Nutrient loading reaching waterways — indicator of water quality pressure |
| | Sediment Export | Erosion delivery to stream networks |

:::

::: {.callout-note style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
**Why export/risk, not retention amount?** For nitrogen, sediment, and coastal, we report the direct physical quantity reaching waterways/shore — the thing people actually experience — rather than a derived retention *amount*, which can rise simply because land conversion generates more to intercept, not because filtering improved.
:::

::: {.notes}
- These 5 are the hotspot-defining set: a cell qualifies as a hotspot if it's in the worst 5% for one of these. Three additional ratio variables (nitrogen retention ratio, sediment retention ratio, coastal risk reduction ratio) are modeled from the same InVEST runs and appear elsewhere as secondary/contextual variables, but do not define hotspot status — export and risk are the direct, unambiguous-direction quantities.
- Service selection follows Chaplin-Kramer et al. (2019) — these cover the broadest human-nature interdependence dimensions InVEST can model globally at consistent resolution.
- If asked why ratios aren't part of the hotspot definition: export/risk tells you what's actually reaching people; a retention ratio can improve or decline for reasons unrelated to local ecological function (e.g., upstream/downstream redistribution) — Becky's call, not a data limitation.
:::

## Socioeconomic Context: The WHO Input Layers

![Four gridded socioeconomic layers joined to each 10km cell. Population density and GDP are structurally high across all hotspot types; HDI and Gini are the variables that separate the two exposure typologies in the WHO analysis.](../../outputs/plots/maps/global_socioeconomic_context_map.png){height="580px" fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
- Population and GDP: universal signal — hotspot cells are denser and wealthier than background across all 5 hotspot-defining services. Not a distinguishing feature of any service type; just reflects where ecosystem services matter to people.
- HDI and GINI: the discriminating variables — coastal services cluster in higher-HDI settings; terrestrial provisioning services cluster in lower-HDI, higher-inequality settings.
- All four layers are 2020 values — a temporal mismatch with the 1992–2020 change window. Acknowledged limitation.
:::

## Spatial Framework & Analytical Groupings

[*Analysis unit: ~1.3 million 100 km² equal-area cells (IUCN AOO 10km grid) — results aggregated across four groupings*]{style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

![Four analytical groupings used throughout: World Bank regions, income groups, WWF biomes, and national boundaries.](../../outputs/maps/context_groupings_map.png){width="88%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
- The 10km equal-area grid is the key methodological choice: it puts large and small ecosystems on equal footing (no size bias).
- World Bank regions → geopolitical framing for policy audiences.
- Income groups → equity and adaptive capacity lens.
- Biomes → ecological framing for conservation audiences.
- Country → operational scale for national policy.
- Using all four avoids the arbitrary choice of a single aggregation and lets patterns emerge at multiple scales.
:::

---

## Why Two Pathways?

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.84em; align-items: flex-start;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Path A — Pixel-level (300m)
*Compare first, then aggregate*

- Each pixel compared 1992 → 2020 at native resolution
- Results summed to regions after comparison
- Preserves every individual gain and loss
- **Used for:** WHAT — global and regional trajectories

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Path B — 10km equal-area grid
*Aggregate first, then compare*

- 300m rasters summarised into ~1.3M equal-area cells (100km² each) *before* computing change
- Equal-area projection: every cell = 100km² regardless of latitude
- Standardised units enable global hotspot ranking
- **Used for:** WHERE, WHO, WHY — hotspot detection and profiling

:::
:::

::: {.callout-note style="font-size: 0.75em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
**Why not one path?** Averaging Path B cell values up to broad regions causes sign divergence between absolute and percentage change in some services — a MAUP artefact. Path A avoids this by never passing through an intermediate grid step.
:::

::: {.notes}
- This is the slide that explains the design decision that generates the most questions. The key is: the ORDER of aggregation vs. differencing matters.
- Path A: diff → aggregate. Path B: aggregate → diff. Different questions, different orders.
- The MAUP artefact: Jerónimo discovered this empirically — in some cases N export showed a positive SPC at the regional level via Path B but a negative absolute change via Path A. Both were mathematically correct at their respective scales. This is not an error; it is a genuine scale-dependence finding.
- Equal-area: a lat/lon grid at 10 arc-minutes would have cells ~50% smaller near 60°N than near the equator. The IUCN AOO equal-area grid removes that bias.
:::

## Key Metrics

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Symmetric Percentage Change (SPC)

<div style="font-size:0.75em">
$$\text{SPC} = \frac{T_{2020} - T_{1992}}{(|T_{2020}| + |T_{1992}|) / 2} \times 100$$
</div>

Normalised for baseline size; symmetric around zero; cross-service comparable. Bounded −200% (total loss) to +200% (new emergence).

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Hotspot Definition
- **Relative** — ranked within each service's own distribution, not an absolute threshold
- **Most adverse 5%** per service *(direction is service-specific)*
- **Compound Risk** = 2+ services in worst-5% in the same cell
- Puts large ecosystems and small remnants on equal footing

:::
:::

---

## Land Cover Change Analysis

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.82em;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Deriving LCC Metrics
- **Two endpoints**: ESA CCI (1992) → C3S (2020) at 300 m
- **Pontius contingency matrix** — separates Gross Loss, Gross Gain, and Exchange *(net change masks simultaneous loss and gain)*
- Per-pixel temporal comparison, then aggregated to the same 10 km equal-area grid
- Five drivers: forest loss, cropland expansion, urban expansion, wetland loss, grassland conversion

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Co-occurrence Design
- **Symmetric threshold**: ES worst-5% (SPC) vs. LCC top-5% (gross conversion magnitude), on the same 10 km grid
- **Key question**: what share of ES hotspot cells co-occur with intense conversion — and what share don't? That complement is the *attribution gap*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- The Pontius approach matters: net change (forest in 1992 minus forest in 2020) would miss simultaneous clearing and regrowth in the same cell. Gross Loss captures what was converted regardless of what regrew.
- Both thresholds operate on the same grid so the comparison is apples-to-apples.
- The ~63.3% gap is a spatial co-occurrence finding, not a causal partition — moderate LCC may still be present in those cells, just below the top-5% threshold. The 36.7% that does overlap is a risk ratio of 7.3 (odds ratio 10.9) — a strong, consistent positive association, true for every one of the five drivers individually.
:::

---

## Statistical Analysis: KS Tests + Cliff's Delta

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Hotspot cells** vs. **Median-background cells**
(47.5th–52.5th percentile of ES change — business-as-usual)

Test variables:
- Population density (GHS-POP 2020)
- GDP (gridded, 2020)
- Human Development Index (HDI)
- Gini coefficient

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Two-step interpretation:**

1. *KS statistic + FDR-corrected p-value* → Do distributions differ?
2. *Cliff's Delta (δ)* → Direction and magnitude

Cliff's Delta = probability that a random hotspot cell has a **higher** value than a random background cell.
δ > 0: hotspot higher; δ < 0: hotspot lower.

**Large-n correction**: background = median 5% of landscape, not the full 1.5M-cell distribution.

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Why median background, not global mean? The comparison isolates what is distinctive about *intense* decline vs. *typical, stable* conditions.
- Cliff's Delta is the practical companion to KS: KS with tens of thousands of hotspot cells will be "significant" for almost any difference. Delta tells you the magnitude.
- δ = 0: distributions fully overlap (random chance). δ = ±1: complete separation. Our range: +0.52 to +0.64 for Pop/GDP (universal across all 5 services).
- **On FDR (if asked):** Running 25 tests at once (5 services × 5 covariates: population, GDP, HDI, GINI, agricultural field size) means ~1 would appear significant by chance alone. FDR correction adjusts the bar across all 25 together to limit false alarms. That 24/25 pass even after correction means the signal is real — the correction barely changed anything. The one non-significant result (Coastal Risk × agricultural field size, p_adj=0.44) makes ecological sense: coastal risk is structurally decoupled from small-plot agricultural landscapes.
:::

# WHO: Exposed Populations {background-color="#007930"}

## WHO: Two Socioeconomic Typologies

![Cliff's Delta (δ) for all 5 services × socioeconomic variables. Orange = hotspot cells higher; green = hotspot cells lower.](../../outputs/plots/ks/directionality_cliffs_delta.png){height="370px" fig-align="center"}

```{=html}
<div class="stat-row">
  <div class="stat-callout">
    <span class="stat-value">+0.52 to +0.64</span>
    <span class="stat-label">Population & GDP — universal across all 5 services</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Higher-development — Coastal Risk
Higher HDI (δ +0.29), modest inequality rise (GINI δ +0.08). Declines concentrate in dense, developed coastlines — built infrastructure expansion is the plausible driver.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Lower-development, higher-inequality — the other four
Nitrogen export, sediment export, pollination, nature access: higher inequality (GINI δ +0.22–0.30), lower-to-neutral HDI (δ −0.01 to −0.08). Populations most exposed tend to be more socially vulnerable and generally less developed.

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Two typologies, not three — the old "retention ratio" typology is gone because ratios are no longer one of the hotspot-defining services being tested here (they're secondary context elsewhere in the paper, not part of this 25-test KS design).
- Population and GDP: universal, not distinguishing — hotspots are embedded in human landscapes across the board, all 5 services.
- Agricultural field size (Mehrabi et al.) does NOT cleanly distinguish these typologies the way HDI/GINI do — small effect sizes (−0.06 to +0.12) relative to the ~0.6 population/GDP effect. Pollination specifically shows near-zero agricultural enrichment (δ=0.01) — it is NOT concentrated in agricultural zones the way intuition might suggest.
- Policy: one-size-fits-all fails across both typologies.
- ~2 minutes
:::

# WHY: The Monitoring Gap {background-color="#004D1E"}

## WHY: What Land Cover Change Looked Like, 1992–2020

![Net land cover conversion intensity 1992–2020. Red = net conversion from natural to transformed landscapes; green = net recovery. The Amazon arc, Central and West Africa, and Southeast Asian archipelagos dominate the signal.](../../outputs/plots/maps/global_lcc_net_change_map.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
- This is the spatial pattern of LC change. The question the next slide addresses: do ES decline hotspots land in the same cells as this conversion?
- This map looks dramatic — and it turns out to be a real, strong signal: the attribution gap analysis shows ES decline is significantly more likely where conversion is most intense. The gap is about *coverage* (how much of ES decline this signal reaches), not about whether the signal is real. Current numbers as of the 2026-09-03 export/risk reversal: 63.3% gap, 36.7% co-occurrence.
- Keep this slide brief — it's setup for the gap finding, not the main result.
:::

---

## WHY: A Strong Signal, Limited Reach

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Land cover conversion hotspots (top 5% intensity, all 5 drivers). This is the full conversion footprint, not filtered to ES-hotspot status — 136,468 cells (9.0% of the grid), vs. 189,932 ES hotspot cells.](../../outputs/plots/maps/global_lcc_driver_hotspots_map.png){width="72%" fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Percentage of ES hotspot cells co-occurring with top 5% of each land cover conversion driver, per service.](../../outputs/plots/drivers/heatmap_driver_overlap_pct.png){width="72%" fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### The Signal
- **36.7% of ES hotspot cells** co-occur with intense (top 5%) land cover conversion from any of 5 drivers combined (at the 10km grid scale) — a risk ratio of **7.3** (odds ratio 10.9, 95% CI 10.81–11.08)
- Correct chance baseline for a 5-driver union: 9.0% of the grid (not the naive ~5% for a single driver — the drivers overlap each other spatially)
- Holds for **every driver individually**: risk ratios from 4.3 (Grassland Gain) to 94.6 (Cropland Expansion) — no offsetting or negative driver

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Interpreting the Gap
- Even so, **63.3%** of ES hotspot cells do NOT co-occur with any of the 5 drivers — this is a coverage limit, not an absence of relationship
- The 63.3% does **not** mean those cells had zero land cover change — many had moderate conversion *below* the top-5% threshold
- **Important:** this is a co-occurrence finding, not a causal partition — the current design cannot distinguish mechanisms
- Conversion detection is a trustworthy signal where present, but it alone still misses most ES decline

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- The attribution gap: we compare the top 5% of ES decline cells against the union of the top 5% of land cover conversion cells across 5 drivers — intense vs. intense.
- 36.7% of ES hotspot cells co-occur with the intense-LCC union — risk ratio 7.3, odds ratio 10.9 (95% CI 10.81–11.08). We lead with risk ratio on the slide (more intuitive: "X times more likely"); odds ratio is the more commonly reported statistic if asked.
- Current as of the 2026-09-03 export/risk reversal (`docs/pipeline_reference.md` row B5) — the hotspot set is now the 5 direct export/risk services (nitrogen export, sediment export, coastal risk, pollination, nature access), not the earlier 8-service or retention/protection framing. Numbers moved slightly from the pre-reversal 5-service figures (34.5%/65.5%) purely because the hotspot *set* changed, not because the land-cover driver data did — the driver-union footprint itself (136,468 cells, 9.0% of grid) is framework-independent.
- The gap: those cells may still have moderate LCC, just not in the most intense 5% of any driver. We still cannot say "degradation is happening without conversion" — that's overclaiming what the spatial overlay can show — but we CAN now say conversion, where intense, is a real and strong predictor.
- Policy message: categorical land cover monitoring is trustworthy where it fires, but it still only reaches about a third of severe ES decline — you need direct ES monitoring to catch the rest.
- ~2 minutes
:::

# Synthesis {background-color="#004D1E"}

## Synthesis: The Four Pillars

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

| Pillar | Finding | Policy Implication |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **WHAT** | Ecosystem services declined measurably 1992–2020; absolute and proportional losses are decoupled by region | Change is real and geographically structured |
| **WHERE** | 190K hotspot cells cluster in Latin America & Caribbean (1.58×) and East Asia & Pacific (1.21×); lower-middle-income countries bear **1.8×** disproportionate burden | Geographic prioritization is feasible; equity lens is essential |
| **WHO** | Two typologies: coastal risk (higher HDI, modest inequality rise), the other four services (higher inequality, lower/neutral HDI); **3.1 billion** in-situ, **7.6 billion (96.7%)** connected via downstream/travel pathways | Typology-specific policy responses; scale demands systemic action |
| **WHY** | ES hotspots co-occur with intense (top 5%) land cover conversion at **36.7%** — a risk ratio of **7.3** (odds ratio 10.9), true for every one of 5 drivers individually; but **63.3%** still show no such overlap — indicating categorical land-cover monitoring alone is insufficient for comprehensively tracking ES decline | Conversion monitoring is a reliable signal where present, but must be paired with direct ES monitoring for the majority of cases |

: {tbl-colwidths="[8,52,40]"}

:::

**How to read:** All cells shown are already in the global top 5% — even the lightest boxes represent severe change. A **wide box** means hotspot severity is highly variable within the group (some cells near the threshold, others near complete functional loss). A **narrow box** means intensities are consistently high. Latin America [3] shows the widest and most intense boxes for Nature Access and Pollination — not just more hotspots, but more variable and more severe ones.

- This chart answers: within the hotspot cells, are they uniformly intense or highly variable?
- Latin America dominates — high severity AND high variability. Some cells approaching SPC of -200% (near-complete loss) for Nature Access and Pollination.
- Direction matters: negative SPC = declining provision (Pollination, Nature Access); positive SPC = increasing export/risk (N_export, Sed_export).

## Appendix: Technical Methods — Key Decisions

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.74em; align-items: flex-start;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Spatial standardisation
- InVEST rasters are in **WGS84** — pixel area varies with latitude
- **Volumetric services** (N export, Sed export): pre-normalised to **per hectare** before extraction, correcting for latitude-dependent pixel size
- **Index and ratio services** (Pollination, Retention Ratios, Nature Access, Coastal Risk): **dimensionless** — area correction would introduce spurious latitudinal gradients; not applied
- **Coastal Risk** (`C_Risk` = `Rt`): wave energy **per linear metre of shoreline** — not an area-based quantity; no per-ha correction

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Aggregation at the grid-cell level
- All ES rasters extracted to 10km grid using **mean** (not sum)
- Rasters are already per-ha → mean gives a valid, comparable per-ha rate across equal-area cells
- For hotspot detection: SPC(mean, mean) = SPC(sum, sum) for equal-area cells — rankings are identical regardless of choice
- **Socioeconomic variables** (Population, GDP) use **sum** — these are absolute counts/totals, a different interpretation

### Equal-area grid
- IUCN AOO 10km grid uses an **equal-area projection**, not lat/lon
- Every cell = exactly 100 km² regardless of latitude
- Makes cross-regional comparisons valid without polar distortion

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- This slide is a Q&A backup — not shown in the main flow.
- The per-hectare correction question comes up because InVEST runs in WGS84 for most services. The key point: correction was applied where it's meaningful (absolute quantities), not applied where it would distort (dimensionless values).
- The mean vs sum question: pragmatically, it doesn't affect hotspot results because SPC normalizes the values. The choice matters more for interpretability of the grid-cell values.
- Equal-area point: a standard lat/lon grid at 10 arc-minutes has cells ~50% smaller at 60°N than at the equator — that would bias hotspot counts toward the tropics by area alone.
:::

### Key Publications & Methods
- Chaplin-Kramer et al. (2019) *Science*: global NCP baseline — this paper extends it
- Pontius & Millones (2011) + Pontius (2022): land cover change transition matrix methodology
- Cliff (1993): Cliff's Delta effect size for ordinal data
- Benjamini & Hochberg (1995): false discovery rate correction
- Andam et al. (2008): ecosystem service spillover effects
- Kolmogorov & Smirnov: non-parametric distribution comparison
